articles.title: Contract: Deadly Delights - The Witcher 3 Guide - IGN
articles.summary: Contract: Deadly Delights is a Side Quest in Novigrad with a suggested level of 15. This Side Quest seems like a standard monster hunt on its surface, but
articles.body:
Contract: Deadly Delights is a Side Quest in Novigrad with a suggested level of 15. This Side Quest seems like a standard monster hunt on its surface, but becomes much more complex once you start digging into the story.

To help you complete it with ease, here's IGN's complete guide to Contract: Deadly Delights, including key character interactions, important choices, and the final quest reward. We'll also look at combat tips, used for getting the Succubus Mutagen.

Contract: Deadly Delights can be started in Novigrad, at the notice board near The Golden Sturgeon. Look for the paper that says "Contract Issued by the Temple Guard of the City of Novigrad" to start.

There's a guard post essentially across the street from your current location. Head over to speak to the guard to learn more about what's been ravaging members of the Temple Guard.

You'll be sent over to the dock to speak to the Temple Guard's medic and learn more about the monster. After talking to the medic to clues about what type of monster it is, head to the crime scene to investigate further.

Use your Witcher Senses at the crime scene to find hoof prints. Follow the hoof prints towards Crippled Kate's, a brothel, and make your way inside.

Talk to the owner at Crippled Kate's; unsurprisingly, she'll be hesitant to talk about the murdered guards. You have a few options here:

Use Axii to fool the madam into telling you that the brothel has been working with a Succubus, receiving a key to her house.

If you can't use a high-level Axii Sign, head back outside the back door of the brothel and use your Witcher Senses to find a perfume bottle. Follow the scent trail until it leads you to a house with a baffled character outside of it. Examining the townsperson will reveal that there's a Succubus, which'll net you a little experience.

The room you need in the house is on the second floor. If you don't have the key, you'll need to scale the neighbour's property and work your way in from above.

Inside the target room, you'll need to decide whether to kill the Succubus, called Salma, or let her leave the city. If you let her leave the city, you'll receive a Succubus Trophy and the Silver Sword Maugrim.

If you kill her, you have a chance to get the Succubus Mutagen, which is needed for the Succubus Decoction. There are only two chances in the game to get it. It's not a must-have, but if you want to create all Decoctions , you'll need to make the tough choice for one of the two.

To kill Salma, you'll need to avoid fire blasts, while striking with heavy attacks. She's not particularly tanky, but her fire attacks do hurt, so Quen can help keep you alive if you get backed into a corner.

When you've made your decision, return to the initial quest-giving guard to collect your reward and finish the Side Quest.

The final reward for this Side Quest will be your negotiated rate, and then 270 x experience on top of this. Contract: Deadly Delight Complete

articles.body:
Contract: Lord of the Wood is a Novigrad Side Quest with a suggested level of 25. It's an investigation-heavy Contract, with a monetary reward that can be increased in negotiations if you're so inclined.

To help you defeat the beast at the heart of this Side Quest, here's IGN's complete guide to Contract: Lord of the Wood, including how to complete the investigation and what you can expect to get as a reward.

To start, the paper Contract: Devil in the Woods can be picked up from the noticeboard at either Cunny of the Goose or the refugee district in the outskirts of Novigrad. This notice will inform you that something malicious seems to be stalking through the nearby woods.

Talk to the halfling Brean Hotsch at Cunny of the Goose. Brean will describe how he hired three dwarves for logging work in the woods, then share that only one of them made it back alive after some sort of attack.

After talking to Hotsch, talk to the nearby survivor of the attacks. There won't be much to learn here -- howls were heard, but there isn't a visual description of the creature.

Head to the Hotsch's woodcutter's hut in the woods to the east of the starting location.

After arriving, use your Witcher senses to find the clues from the woodcutter's wagon. Follow the trail of the wagon using Witcher senses. You may encounter Nekkers , and a Nekker warrior along the trail.

After finding the wagon, investigate the site using your Witcher Senses. There will be two sets of blood stains, footprints, and claws on a rock. After examining those clues, your Witcher Senses will show the footprints leading towards a dwarf. The set of bloodstains will lead to another dwarf.

From these clues, Geralt will determine that there's a Leshen monster at the heart of this Contract.

Head to each map marker until you find the Leshen totem. After destroying the totem, the Leshen will appear.

After dealing with the Leshen, head back to Hotsch to collect your reward.

When you wrap up this Side Quest, you'll receive 250 x experience, along with your negotiated chunk of cash.

articles.title: Riders on the Storm - Cyberpunk 2077 Guide - IGN
articles.summary: Riders on the Storm is just one of the many Side Jobs available in the Badlands. This Cyberpunk 2077 walkthrough for Riders on the Storm will guide you through
articles.body:
Riders on the Storm is just one of the many Side Jobs available in the Badlands . This Cyberpunk 2077 walkthrough for Riders on the Storm will guide you through meeting with Panam, saving Saul, and tips for romancing her at the end of the mission.

Use the links below to skip to key steps:

This side job is part of the Panam Romance Guide chain of missions. If you intend to romance this character, keep an eye out for a few specific interactions.

After waiting 12 hours in-game, you’ll get a call from Panam asking for help. Meet with her at an Aldecaldos camp and offer to help her.

Follow Panam over to a car where several Aldecaldos members are planning the next steps of the mission. This leads to Mitch giving you a shard to check out a Wraith camp where Saul is being held prisoner.

You'll soon use a drone to observe the base. Scan the following objectives to complete this portion of Riders on the Storm:

Once you’ve finished the drone objectives, disconnect from the shard when given a chance. You can engage in optional dialogue now with the other Aldecaldos remaining near the car. Otherwise, head over to Panam and Mitch to get a SuperJet injector from Mitch.

Now hop into the van they’re leaning against and drive with Panam to the Raffen Shiv camp. After parking the van, you’ll need to sneak into the camp.

Run to the left of the camp along a cliff to sneak inside the camp quietly. You can follow this around the back to reach the main building without running into many guards.

Don't Miss: Once you're inside the base, you can find a Wraith Boss Hunter enemy near the entrance - use your scanner to identify them. Neutralize this enemy and loot them to get the Problem Solver Iconic Power SMG.

Use our guide to all the Cyberpunk 2077 Iconic Weapons to find the rest.

The main large garage door doesn’t require any attribute levels to open either. After entering the warehouse from here, follow the left wall until you reach the stairs heading down. There are two distracted guards down here that you can walk past.

Continue through the two sets of doors until you find someone at a computer to take out. The next room has Saul strapped to a chair where you can inject him with the SuperJet. You can either exit the way you came in or leave through a maintenance tunnel using Technical Ability 9. Once you make it outside, Panam will pull up with a van for both you and Saul to get into.

Panam will eventually park near a building that you can hide in for shelter. Head to the back where a fuse box is that you can interact with to turn on the power. Saul will mention that it’s getting cold, leading to the next objective. Panam will ask you to head outside and check the external panel to fix the heat. After interacting with the panel outside, return inside.

Sit down on the couch near Panam and listen to Saul talk. A timed conversation option will appear: “Let’s take it easy - you’re both tired.”

Then, defend Panam if you’re following the Panam Romance Guide , by picking “Shitty idea, Panam’s right.” The next dialogue choice unique to the Nomad Life Path continues to support her: “Rather not follow in the Bakkers’ footsteps.” Follow the choices below to further your connection with her.

”And? This any better?” or “[NOMAD] Hard to get used to”

Pleased with your stay, ma’am? - Timed choice, likely not required.

You’d be more comfortable with your shoes off, ma’am.”

Either choice: “[Touch Panam’s thigh] Got a few ideas” or “You choose. Customer’s always right.

Panam will start to doze off and Johnny Silverhand will briefly appear. After V wakes up, head outside where Panam and Saul are waiting. Continue speaking with Panam as she wanders over to her bike. Eventually, she’ll mention your reward, but before you grab it, stay near her. People trying to romance Panam will have a timed choice here, “[Stop Panam] Wait. About last night…”

Grab the Overwatch iconic weapon leaning against the other bike. If you grab the rifle before waiting to stop Panam, you may miss the timed choice.

After speaking with Johnny, the side job, Riders on the Storm will be complete.

articles.title: Best Bethesda RPGs, Ranked
articles.summary: The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel has officially been revealed, but what are the best Bethesda RPGs you can play now? From Fallout 3 to Skyrim, here are our picks.
articles.body:
The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel has finally been revealed . But that's still ahead in the future. What about the past? It’s rare that a developer becomes synonymous with a single genre, but Bethesda has its signature style so locked down it’s a wonder we don’t just call the entire field of first-person open-world Western RPGs “Skyrimlikes” or “Oblivionvanias.” In the three decades since The Elder Scrolls: Arena debuted, Bethesda Game Studios has emerged as a juggernaut in the triple-A space, earning a rabid fanbase, massive sales, and a $7.5 billion acquisition from Microsoft, solely on the strength of its tried and true design principles.

Bethesda’s been responsible for some big hits and even bigger misses over the years, and since the shocking (but not really) release of The Elder Scrolls: Oblivion Remaster has us all rethinking our long-calcified tier-lists, we thought it was time to take a fresh look at ranking the studio’s output.

Before we start, we should clarify that we’re strictly talking about Bethesda’s trademark RPGs on this list. The extremely mid Elder Scrolls spinoffs, like the co-op focused Battlespire and swashbuckling action-adventure Redguard, need not apply here. Nor do mobile games like The Elder Scrolls Blades and Fallout Shelter , although I’ve definitely got a soft spot for the latter game’s dark humor and infinite armies of cartoon dwellers captured in the charming Vault Boy style.

No, this list is for the heavy hitters, the sprawling, prestige sandboxes that immediately come to mind when one thinks of a capital B, capital G “Bethesda Game,” though admittedly we’re starting out on a rather humble foot with…

The first entry in the franchise isn’t last because it’s a bad game, it’s last because nobody knew what they were doing. The Bethesda of 1994 had basically only made sports and Terminator games, and Arena was kind of a mix of both. Originally, you traveled the world competing in medieval gladiator battles, doing the odd sidequest on the side. The developers quickly realised it would be a cool idea if your fighters could walk around the cities, talk to the people who live there, and dive into incredibly difficult dungeons on their behalf.

The result is an impressive little first-person RPG that’s very much of its era, a “where-the-hell-do-I-go-em-up” in the vein of Ultima Underworld and Might and Magic. Arena has loads of arcane systems and randomized loot, meandering, maddening, sidequests, and extremely clunky movement that will make you forget everything you’ve ever learned about using a mouse.

And given how bad the combat is, the kind of stats-based melee that sees you visually landing hit after hit on rampaging skeletons only to deal no damage thanks to a dice roll, maybe it’s a good thing the developers dropped the whole “gladiator” concept for Arena. Less fortunately, they didn’t drop it fast enough to change the title, since all the marketing materials were already printed up. The best they could do was tack on a “chapter one” and make it seem like the game was part of a larger saga about all-knowing Elder Scrolls .

Declaring your debut the start of a new franchise is a gutsy move that more often than not ends in failure, but the extremely flawed Arena was still successful enough to set Bethesda on a path that would fulfill its prediction, and boldly go beyond.

With every new BGS game comes rumors and discourse on whether this will be the one that finally ditches their aging “Gamebryo” engine, or at least updates the notoriously inefficient cell-based framework beyond its well-known limits. Starfield did not . “Creation Engine 2.0” might have a fancy new name and a pretty new animation pipeline, but at the end of the day you’re still staring at a loading screen every time you step into a store.

The NASApunk sci-fi setting was a welcome departure from the low-tech locales of Tamriel and the Wasteland, even though it’s starting to wear out its welcome, but it’s ill-suited for Bethesda’s style. They’re great at creating one big connected world, full of discoveries, nooks and crannies, and intricately staged skeletons with nearby flavor notes. Instead, Starfield boasts 1,000 procedurally generated planets with what feels like a dozen different points of interest repeated between them.

Now, we've solved more than a few dragon claw puzzles in our day, but somehow that never felt as aggravating as landing on a new planet and stumbling across another abandoned cryo lab or mine. Dear god, the mines. If you’re bored in a samey Draugr dungeon, you can just walk to something cool around the corner. But in Starfield you’re just kinda stuck dejectedly wiping out the pirates, hoofing it back to your spaceship, and blasting off with a sigh.

It might seem harsh to place Starfield so close to something as primitive as Arena, but it’s easier to forgive the shortcomings of a gallant first effort from an inexperienced team than those of a $200 million triple-A behemoth that promised the moon and failed to deliver.

One reason the procedural generation in Starfield is such a bummer is that Bethesda has so much experience with it going way, way back. In fact, its second RPG ever is one of the most impressive feats of algorithmic open world creation that ever existed, and it came out in 1997.

The map in Skyrim translates to about 15 square miles, and that’s actually on the smaller side compared to games that came out in its wake. Breath of the Wild and Grand Theft Auto 5’s are both around 30 square miles , give or take. The Elder Scrolls: Daggerfall is 80,000 square miles , roughly the size of Great Britain. It’ll take you 69 hours to walk across the entire thing, though it’ll go slightly quicker if you’re okay with staring at the back of this horse's head for days on end as your precious time on Earth slowly whittles away.

The world is vast, sparse, and kind of ugly, but it’s definitely not empty. The Iliac Bay area contains nine distinct climates, 44 different political regions, and 15,000 points of interest scattered throughout. We’re talking 4,000 dungeons and 5,000 cities or towns populated with hundreds of quests and non-player-characters. Needless to say, there’s a touch of wonky proc-gen involved.

But what good is a huge world if it’s a slog to move around in? The dungeon-crawling combat is only slightly improved, though the debut of the series’ trademark “improve your stats as you use their skills” progression system is definitely appreciated. In Daggerfall, it’s the experience above ground that made the biggest leap in quality. You can buy houses and boats, join guilds, steal and murder to your heart's content and deal with the consequences. While it’s all relatively simple and extremely opaque, the opportunities for immersion within Daggerfall almost make you wish you could explore it with a friend or two. Almost.

You might be confused as to why Fallout 76 is on this list at all, given that it’s more of a live service, multiplayer looter-shooter than an epic, story-driven RPG experience, and if you haven’t played it for a while that’s totally fair. The game was a straight-up disaster at launch , omitting hand-crafted dialogue and non-player characters in the hopes that griefing online randos would be able to provide the flavor that makes Fallout’s wastelands so worthwhile. This was a mistake, to put it mildly, and just one of many. From aggravating loot limits and endless crafting to questionable pricing practices, Fallout 76 was a dud when it debuted in 2018, thanks in no small part to a grueling development cycle that plagued the project from the start.

Things have changed, however . The Wastelanders update added voiced NPCs to the experience, so many in fact that technically it has the most characters of any game in the whole series. Whether they have anything worthwhile to say is still up for debate but they’re there, along with tweaks to the loot system and overall experience that make it less of a slog and more of a passable RPG to play with friends. The game has developed a healthy following, especially in the wake of Amazon’s hit Fallout TV series, but even so, it’s hard to rank Fallout 76 very high given the existence of the superior Elder Scrolls Online, Bethesda’s long-running MMO that only failed to make the cut here because it was developed out of house by Zenimax Online Studios.

Fallout 76’s pivot towards live-service, revenue-generating, trend-chasing slop gave fans grave doubts about Bethesda’s stewardship of the Fallout franchise, but they didn’t exist in a vacuum. Discontent had been brewing for a long time, even as sales skyrocketed.

At 25 million copies sold, Fallout 4 is the most successful game in the series by a wide, wide margin, beyond the wildest dreams of Tim Cain and the rest of the Interplay/Black Isle crew that created the original isometric RPGs in the ’90s, though that success comes with a cost. Streamlined gameplay and welcome quality-of-life features can turn a niche cult classic into a mainstream blockbuster, but balancing that accessibility without sacrificing depth and complexity is no easy task. Fallout 4 fails in that regard.

First, the good: Fallout 4 feels great . The movement and shooting feels crisp and responsive compared to its clunky predecessors, and the Commonwealth is more than a worthy environment to explore. A new system that allows you to design and build your own settlements is an impressive addition to Bethesda’s aging tech, though it’s a coin flip as to whether you’ll find it fun or a complete waste of time. The game looks and sounds spectacular, and was arguably the most polished launch product Bethesda produced since… ever . Some of its expansions, particularly Far Harbor, seemed to capture that old Fallout feeling, and there’s at least one all-time classic character to emerge out of the crowd of Bostonian blandness and micromanaging Minutemen in the form of android private eye Nick Valentine.

The storyline, revolving around high-tech synthetic humans teleporting from a crisp and clean underground lab, is at odds with the grungy atompunk flavor of the Fallout universe, and the bizarre twist involving the identity of your character’s missing son was both blindingly obvious and incredibly dumb. The whole experience feels like a Fallout-flavored theme park ride, plopping you in power armor to face off with a deathclaw within the first hour of gameplay. From there, the game parades you through a series of shallow choices and uninteresting factions until you pick who you’re going to side with and watch the uninspired endings play out.

The biggest detriment to the game has to be the dialogue system. The first Fallout, famously, allows for all sorts of freedom in how the Vault Dweller interacts with the world around them, from monosyllabic grunts to talking the super mutant Master into unaliving himself in the final boss battle. Fallout 4, on the other hand, made the dubious decision to voice all of our protagonist’s interaction, severely limiting their options. Even worse, the four choices offered in response to any situation usually boil down to nice, rude, neutral, and “tell me more.” It’s a disappointing devolution of the RPG formula, but not entirely unsurprising given Bethesda’s first Fallout game.

When Bethesda announced it had purchased the rights to the dormant Fallout franchise in 2004, fans went nuclear. For some, Fallout seemed like a perfect fit for the devs that wrote the book on systemic open world sandboxes, but there was a sizeable contingent of gatekeeping grognards who were a little more wary, warning that the Bethesda crew would tone done the anarchic spirit of the first two games for a more bland experience in hopes of capturing a more casual audience. The end result was a little bit of both .

The revival starts out extremely strong, with an opening sequence that begins with your character exiting the womb and then gives a quick crash course in all that life inside Vault 101 has to offer, from bullies to birthday parties. The intro also serves as a tutorial for the V.A.T.S. system, maybe Bethesda’s most brilliant addition to the franchise. The isometric, turn-based Fallout games allowed your character to target individual body parts in combat, allowing for agonizing and often hilarious precision shots. In the leap to first person, BSG compensates for their somewhat muddy controls by letting us freeze time and select precisely where we’d like our strikes to land in one of the most elegant translations of a game mechanic from 2D to 3D ever.

Not everything in Fallout 3 is as successful as V.A.T.S., however. The Capital Wasteland is a fantastic map filled with recognizably ruined national landmarks, but it’s also stuffed with repetitive encounters in subways and sewers awash in a hideous green filter that was all the rage in the early aughts. There are meaningful choices with megaton consequences that ultimately railroad you into an utterly ludicrous ending scenario that requires you to sacrifice your life to radiation while your radiation-immune supermutant friend watches from a safe distance A conclusion that was so derided, Bethesda would eventually patch it by way of the Broken Steel DLC.

It’s the very best and very worst of Bethesda’s instincts laid bare, and the awkward friction integrating BGS’s environmental storytelling with Fallout’s anarchic RPG flavor makes vanilla Fallout 3 a rather unpleasant experience today. An excellent alternative is theTale of Two Wastelands mod that fuses Fallout 3 together with Obsidian Entertainment’s fan-favorite Fallout: New Vegas to create a single massive game. Or if that’s too much of a hassle, you could just wait for the all-but-confirmed remake that’s coming in the wake of Oblivion Remastered. Speaking of which…

This was a tough call. Many of Oblivion’s adoring fans might find it blasphemous to be placed before Skyrim, while haters might contest that some of the Fallouts are superior. The truth, as always, is subjective, except for on ranking lists like this, which are infallible, definitive, scientifically determined and legally binding so let’s see how it stacks up.

Oblivion is the foundation of modern Bethesda games . Morrowind, obviously, came before, but it’s notable that Fallout, Starfield, and every Bethesda game (and Bethesda wannabe) since 2006 have used Oblivion as the template rather than its predecessor. The awkward pause and zoom in to start a conversation, the OP dominance of stealth archery, the ramping-up power fantasy designed to make a lowly prisoner feel like the most important being in all of Tamriel… It’s all here in pretty much its final form, though with lots of room for improvement.

The main plot sees you fending off a demonic Daedric invasion alongside a Sean Bean-voiced bastard in a cinematic saga that borrows bigtime vibes from Peter Jackson’s wildly popular Lord of the Rings trilogy. But it’s the sidequests, particularly those involving the guilds, that really elevate Oblivion. They’re all really solid in Skyrim, too, but Oblivion’s individual missions have a lot more going for them.

Instead of Skyrim’s fairly rote assassinations on behalf of the Dark Mother, your devotion to the Dark Brotherhood in Oblivion is tested by specific kill conditions that make you feel like an Argonian Agent 47. Meanwhile, while Skyrim’s introduction to the Thieves Guild effectively amounts to getting approached by a recruiter, in Oblivion, it only exists as shadows and rumors, the only clues to their existence are scattered posters and urban legends. You have to work to seek them out.

So why did we rank Oblivion below Skyrim? Maybe it’s the eye-searing ugly bloom of the XBox 360 era, or the dorky potato-faced characters stumbling through their lines. It could be the ill-conceived progression system that forces you to grind minor skills for fear of losing precious stat points when you level up, or the repetitive trudging through endless Oblivion gates. Of course, all of that can change with a remake.

The Oblivion Remaster goes a long way towards modernizing the game, with a slick UI, gorgeous new graphics, a more forgiving level-up system, and a deeply appreciated sprint button. Gone is the blinding haze of the seventh console generation, replaced with a solid Unreal Engine sheen. Unlike a lot of remasters, Oblivion maintains its awkward charms, for better or for worse.

The enemy scaling is sadly still intact, meaning you’ll find yourself running into gangs of filthy bandits bearing glass and Daedric gear. Most of the frustrating minigames have been retained, and the combat still feels strange by modern standards. But would Oblivion really be Oblivion without the jank? Without expensive horse armor and actors flubbing their lines?

The Oblivion Remaster is still the same game. It might be a little too early to tell if the remaster will be worthy of a higher spot than Skyrim, but there’s a fundamental difference between the two games that’s more than just skin deep.

For all of its triumphs, Skyrim loses a lot of what makes the older Elder Scroll games so special. The quests are more shallow, your character build isn’t as customizable, and your choices matter even less. You can quickly become the leader of every single guild, and the biggest decision of the game is who you want to back in the Skyrim Civil War, which culminates in an epic battle of about 40 dudes clipping into each other outside of Whiterun.

In exchange for the simplification, Skyrim received massive, undeniable improvements to the moment-to-moment gameplay . You can dash across the landscape and glitch hop your way up mountains. Additions like dual wielding and weapon crafting finally make the kinetic act of combat enjoyable in itself, and the brilliant addition of shouts allows you to drop dragons out of the sky and blast guards into the horizon with a single squeeze of a shoulder button. Clearly, the game was designed with controllers in mind, as a glance at the oft-maligned default interface will tell you, but that brings with it a tactile and responsive game feel that Skyrim’s PC-first counterparts lack. Skyrim simply feels better.

But the real secret that separates Skyrim from Oblivion is its space. In past lore, Oblivion’s setting of Cyrodiil was an endless jungle of East Asian and Mesoamerican-influenced aesthetics. In the game itself, it’s basically England. Green forests, grassy fields, and the odd Ayleid Ruin dot a landscape that fails to leave much of an impression compared to Skyrim’s frozen tundra. The mechanical depths of the Dwemer ruins, the hazy valleys of the Rift, and the glaciers of Winterhold, all feel like part of a cohesive whole. Skyrim’s geography becomes second nature as you climb enormous mountains and explore endless caves, all the while knowing that the warm glow of Whiterun at night is just a cozy walk away.

Frankly, it’s a place you wouldn’t mind settling down and living out your days in a comfy Lakeview Manor, raising honey bees with your werewolf wife at your side. It’s no wonder so many people found themselves lost in Skyrim over the years, compelled to purchase the game over and over again with each slightly-improved release. For many, Skyrim and its suite of mods are the first thing to install on any new computer, just so you know it’s there – a true “forever game.”

Skyrim is the game that turned the Elder Scrolls from a successful but nerdy RPG franchise into a blockbuster AAA giant. It’s like comparing Dark Souls to Elden Ring. Similar to Oblivion, Dark Souls is probably the better game on paper, but in terms of impact, the refinement that led to Elden Ring and Skyrim allowed the games to simultaneously expand in scope and reach the widest audience possible. Skyrim isn’t a game you have to recommend with huge caveats to your friend who mostly plays Warzone, it sacrificed just enough of its systems to smooth out its friction points and in the process became an all-time best seller.

This isn’t to say that it should be ranked highly just because it made a ton of money, but rather that it made a ton of money because of how well it struck a balance between accessibility and depth, allowing players of all kinds to immerse themselves in an intricately crafted world and live out that timeless, universal fantasy of slaying dragons. But with all due respect to Skyrim’s successful efforts to make the game accessible to the mainstream, our number one spot goes to the game that achieved the exact opposite.

We couldn’t in good faith leave this list without mentioning the best Fallout game ever made . Even if it was developed by Obsidian, it’s built on Bethesda’s bugs-and-all engine and wouldn’t exist without the other games on this list, even though it’s better than all of them. A near-perfect marriage of old-school sensibility and BGS open-world quirkiness, you don’t want to miss this one, especially if you plan on watching season 2 of the show.

Which brings us to the greatest Bethesda game of all time, coming in hot from the isle of Vvardenfell, it simply must be…

For a game that we’re definitively calling the greatest Elder Scrolls game of all time , it’s far from the most polished or accessible. The combat retains much of the RNG aggravation of earlier games, and The UI, cluttered with resizable windows and long lists of dialogue choices to scroll through, borders on utter madness. It’s almost impossible to believe that people once navigated this monstrosity with nothing but a giant Xbox Duke controller, but indeed they did.

And yet, despite the at-times overwhelming encumbrances of age and complexity, Morrowind is unparalleled when it comes to pure freedom. There are no quest markers or floating arrows on a compass to guide your way, just clues in a dense journal filled with vast amounts of text to click through with hyperlinks. Its spellmaking system, nerfed and eventually eliminated over the years, allows for utterly broken combinations that let you leap between cities and blast across the sky on Boots of Blinding Speed. Characters have seemingly endless amounts of dialogue, spewing forth on screen in massive paragraphs – though if you get tired of reading, you can always end their worthless life. Always.

No NPC is unkillable in Morrowind, not even the essential ones. In most Bethesda games, if you bludgeon a story-integral character to death with the Mace of Molag Bal, they just take a wee nap and rise again to move the story along. Morrowind instead presents you with the haunting yet somehow liberating message: “the thread of prophecy is severed… restore the weave of fate or persist in the doomed world you have created.”

And what a doomed world it is. Vvardenfell is an ashen wonderland where giant insects float among towering fungi and dark elves set up shop in hollowed-out exoskeletons. It borrows more from The Dark Crystal and Dune than it does from Tolkien, a bold, experimental, and organic departure from tropes and tradition. There’s just something magical about Morrowind. Even when later games like ESO return to the region, it never quite hits the same as the original’s rough graphics and smeary textures that render the world as a trippy fusion of Cruelty Squad and Xavier: Renegade Angel.

But that individuality comes at a cost. For every person enamored by riding giant bugs as public transit or reading 36 volumes of a Dunmer god’s wisdom, someone else decided to play Halo 2 instead. Bethesda made a very conscious decision to make Oblivion more inviting, and its investment obviously paid off. Still, it’s hard not to ponder what could have been.

Reflecting on Morrowind, one can’t help but think of Baldur’s Gate 3 – a modernized, uncompromised take on the classic CRPG genre that took the video game world by storm when it was released. BG3 isn’t a retro novelty throwback, nor is it a dumbed-down trend-chasing crowd pleaser. It’s simply what fans of the first two games could have envisioned a long-delayed followup would look like, which begs the question: How would an actual sequel to Morrowind work? And would today’s audience accept it?

Truthfully, the top three Bethesda games are almost entirely interchangeable. You can make a solid argument for them in any order, based on your own personal preferences and, let’s face it, more than a little nostalgia. For us, Morrowind is at the top of this list because there will never, ever be another Bethesda game like it –- but as always, your own personal ranking may vary. So, commence dragonshouting your favorites in the comments below!

articles.title: Netflix's New Series Bass X Machina Finds a Balance Between Western Tropes, Retro-Sci-Fi, and Bloody Violence
articles.summary: Review: Netflix's Bass X Machina revisits the legend of Deputy U.S. Marshal Bass Reeves, adding a steampunk twist to what is essentially an origin story for this version of the lawman.
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for Bass X Machina Episode 1, “Until Then... I'm Bass Reeves.” The full six-episode season is available now on Netflix.

The latest animated production from Studio Mir (Devil May Cry, X-Men '97, My Adventures With Superman, etc.) to make its way to our airwaves… or streaming waves – whatever we’re calling them these days – Bass X Machina is, based on this first episode, a fun and violent excursion into the world of the steampunk Western, but with an eye to Black history. Or rather, alt-history, since this series gives us a Wild West where robots and cyborgs are the norm, even while the face-in-the-dirt killin’ remains as ruthless as ever.

Brian Tyree Henry, who also is an executive producer on the series, voices Bass Reeves, or this world’s version of Bass Reeves, who of course in reality was a historic lawman; an ex-slave who went on to become a Deputy U.S. Marshal, Reeves has been portrayed in movies, TV and elsewhere many times over the years, perhaps most notably in recent years in Damon Lindelof’s Watchmen (where his legend inspired that world’s first superhero, Hooded Justice ).

As the first episode starts, Reeves explains in VO how, after the Civil War, the Union Army was “saddled with thousands of Black soldiers they didn’t know what to do with. And after having known the horrors of war, some of these soldiers didn’t know what to do with themselves.” Some chose the life of the gun in the West, some became Buffalo Soldiers, and “some legendary few… became lawmen.”

Only when we first meet Reeves, he’s a bounty hunter, not a lawman – a fact which is driven home immediately when he shoots two opponents without thinking twice about it. In fact, he’s also part machine, utilizing a steam-powered arm which has replaced his real appendage at some point in his violent history. Quick flashbacks/dreams to some blood-red past event indicate we’ll eventually learn the story of how he came by that arm, but not today.

The action in this first episode is fun and bloody, with a dynamic range of camera moves and angles as Reeves, for starters, shoots the heck out of a gang of crooks during a train heist. Bullets enter (and exit) foreheads with style, while the speed of the racing train and pyrotechnics of a Gatling gun add to the overall excitement of the opening scene. Henry’s Reeves also establishes his general apathy towards his opponents right out of the gate, such as when, after dispatching one fellow’s two brothers, the man cries, “You took my brothers away!” Henry’s Reeves dispassionately responds, “You’re back with ‘em now” before finishing the guy off with a single shot. Dang.

After an opening credits sequence that further hints at Reeves’ origin story, complete with propulsive theme song by Janelle Monáe, the series’ main storyline is established. A scientist named Dr. Eugene Starr has gone missing, apparently into the Native American territory called the Badlands. But not just any scientist: It seems Starr, or someone close to him, has been experimenting on the “magic metal that’s going around” – and using it on people. Whether or not this magic metal is the same substance that has made “boilertech” commonplace in this world is unclear, but regardless, human experimentation is clearly a topic of interest for Reeves, who says that his arm “wasn’t lost. It was stolen.”

Tati Gabrielle voices Dana Starr, a young woman who is the niece of the missing scientist and an engineering genius who winds up playing sidekick to Reeves. She’s able to build handy gadgets while also calculating things like, say, how much time Dr. Starr has left to live after the possibility of “predation, murder, dysentery, despair.” (The answer is three days.) Monáe also voices Reeves’ wife Glory, and we learn that the couple have two sons as well. But Reeves can’t rest – or be a father and husband – while he knows that the key to his past could be lurking out there with Dr. Starr…

Created by LeSean Thomas, who’s also worked on series like Yasuke, Cannon Busters, and Black Dynamite, Bass X Machina finds a nice balance between the Western tropes, retro-sci-fi tech, bloody violence, and animated style. By the time Episode 1 winds down and Reeves and Dana are heading off into the Badlands to begin their journey – one on a horse and the other on a makeshift boilertech scooter – it’s clear that this has not just been the beginning of a beautiful friendship, but also of a cool new animated world.

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Global Release Times
articles.summary: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is just days away, and we have the global release times so you can plan for when you can play in your timezone.
articles.body:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is almost upon us, and while Nintendo has yet to make an official announcement about when the Switch 2 exclusive goes live on the eShop, based on previous release times for the company’s big games, we know what to expect.

Ocarina of Time is expected to launch at midnight local time globally on November 5, which means that yes, the good old New Zealand trick applies if you really want to get ahead of the game (if you’re in North America, a full day early!).

But it’s worth noting that in North America, we’re talking about midnight in the eastern most time zone. So, Zelda goes live at 12am ET on November 5, but 9pm PT on November 4. Make sure you've got enough space on your Switch 2; The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake weighs in at 24.5 GB.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Preview Screenshots

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake global release times:

Denver (Mountain): 10pm MST (November 4)

Chicago (Central): 11pm CST (November 4)

As you can see, you can play Ocarina of Time early if you link your Nintendo Account to another region, or create a new account. This process will be familiar to a number of Switch and Switch 2 owners who have already made new accounts just for moments like this.

There are other things you’ll need to bear in mind if you're doing the New Zealand trick. You’ll need a New Zealand credit card or eShop cards to add funds to your New Zealand Nintendo Account. And if you do that you’ll end up paying over the odds for Ocarina of Time, relative to how much it would cost in USD. So, you’ll need to really, really want to play a day early to fuss over the New Zealand trick.

Nintendo has also announced in-store events at both Nintendo San Francisco and Nintendo New York, if you fancy an old-school midnight launch celebration with fans.

As Nintendo has pulled back the curtain on The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake , we’ve begun to get a better understanding of how this Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive will look and feel to play. IGN has already got you covered with an extensive hands-on preview , as well as a roundup of all the changes we’ve noticed so far compared to the N64 masterpiece.

While you wait for the game to come out, check out a special episode of Nintendo Voice Chat where we dive deeper into our Zelda preview. Meanwhile, we finally have confirmation of who actually developed the Ocarina of Time remake .

articles.title: South of Midnight Creative Director Would Have Turned Off Xbox 'Money Tap' Earlier, Says Funding Was 'Unsustainable'
articles.summary: David Sears, creative director of South of Midnight, said in a recent interview that he was always worried about the previous era of Xbox's infamous development funding "money tap," and admitted he would probably have turned it off earlier.
articles.body:
David Sears, creative director of South of Midnight, said in a recent interview that he was always worried about the previous era of Xbox's infamous development funding "money tap," and admitted he would probably have turned it off earlier.

The Xbox Game Studios-published South of Midnight launched in 2025, seven years after Compulsion Games' previous game came out. While it enjoyed critical acclaim, it failed commercially. Compulsion split from Xbox this year amid CEO Asha Sharma's "reset" of Microsoft's video game business, which has seen thousands of staff lose their jobs, multiple owned studios go independent, and multiple projects canceled.

In an interview with MinnMax , Sears said he was always worried Microsoft's generous funding of South of Midnight would end. “I literally told people, I was like, 'Wow, this could be terrible,’” he said. “Because somebody is going to say one day, 'You know the money tap? We're closing those floodgates.' And that's going to have really traumatic results downstream.”

Next, he was asked if he’d have turned off the tap earlier himself if he was in charge of Xbox, to which he replied: “Yeah, probably.”

“I wanted to make [South of Midnight], no doubt. Obviously, because we made it,” he continued. “Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless. But in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course it was going to have a shocking outcome."

Microsoft bought Compulsion in mid-2018 as part of a spate of acquisitions designed to bolster subscription service Game Pass' day-one offering under previous gaming boss Phil Spencer. That summer, Xbox's ranks were swollen by the arrival of Forza Horizon developer Playground, State of Decay developer Undead Labs, Hellblade developer Ninja Theory, the aforementioned Compulsion Games, then, later that year, inXile and Obsidian. Microsoft also formed a new studio in Santa Monica called The Initiative, which worked on the canceled Perfect Dark reboot. Microsoft acquired Double Fine the following year, in June 2019.

“It’s easy to dissect it now, but at the time I would talk to other directors who would be like, ‘How is this happening? How did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?’ And I would always be like, ‘For now.’ There’s always a night when Rome burns. I didn’t know exactly when it would be but I was always worried about it.

“But to their credit — amazing. I think there’s definitely a corporate Microsoft DNA, but they are vastly different from the Microsoft I knew back in the ‘90s and early 2000s — much more humane, actually. It’s remarkable and commendable.”

Sears went on to praise Microsoft for letting studios spin off from Xbox rather than shut them down, pointing to how Microsoft bought Ensemble Studios only to shut it down after a couple of games. Like Psychonauts developer Double Fine and State of Decay maker Undead Labs, Compulsion Games secured its independence instead of being closed.

Deathloop and Dishonored 2 developer Arkane Lyon, however, is still looking for a buyer as Xbox explores options to split from the studio. Hellblade developer Ninja Theory went through the same process , but didn’t find a buyer and closed as a result.

Earlier this year, Microsoft announced that the next mainline Halo game will be developed by Call of Duty maker Activision , with mass layoffs hitting Halo Studios. Xbox has moved Age of Empires developer World's Edge and Sea of Thieves developer Rare under the Activision umbrella. Microsoft is doubling down on its biggest video game franchises as it works to improve revenue at Xbox and grow its profit margin.

South of Midnight was Compulsion's third game, following Contrast in 2013 and We Happy Few in 2018. It retains ownership of its games and publishing rights despite leaving Xbox.

articles.title: 'Friendslop' Added to the Collins Dictionary, Beaten to Word of the Year by 'Mogging'
articles.summary: Friendslop has been mogged hard by mogging. Friendslop is chopped, and mogging is sigma. It’s cooked, and mogging has been hard mewing in its looksmaxxing era. One is sus and the other is farming aura.
articles.body:
Friendslop has been mogged hard by mogging. Friendslop is chopped, and mogging is sigma. It’s cooked, and mogging has been hard mewing in its looksmaxxing era. One is sus and the other is aura farming.

You might not like it, but that’s what language looks like these days. The Collins dictionary has added a range of new terms from gen alpha slang, including “mogging” — Collins’ word of the year — and “friendslop,” a video game term used to describe a new wave of mess-about-with-your-pals co-op games.

“friendslop (ˈfrɛndˌslɒp) noun a type of low-budget, independently produced video game, designed to be played casually with a group of friends,” is the official new dictionary definition.

It joins words such as “fricy,” which apparently means a food that’s both fruity and spicy. And also the less fun “P(doom)” — (ˈpiːˌduːm) an estimation of the probability that AI will bring about the collapse of human civilization. Lovely.

If you don’t know what mogging means, that opening paragraph was probably nonsensical, but we might as well teach you the language of the youth while you’re here. Mogging means to outshine in any aspect.

There’s height mogging, status mogging, wealth mogging, and looks mogging. There’s probably more mogs that I’m not aware of, but you can basically mog at anything. I mog at Apex Legends, for example. I mog hard.

Alex Beecroft, MD Collins, said: "Collins lexicographers not only track how often words are used, but they also analyse patterns of usage. The selection of ‘mogging' as Collins’ Word of the Year shows how each generation leaves its mark on language.

“It’s a great example of how Gen Z and Gen Alpha have adopted a word and turned it into humorous slang, making the language their own and 'mogging' the rest of us!"

If you’re not familiar with friendslop, arguably the best game in the “genre” released this year with Big Walk . You owe it to yourself to play it. Go in blind and bring friends. It’s unlike anything else.

“Big Walk is full of beautiful emergent moments as you find solutions to cleverly built puzzles and adventure between them in its vast open world,” said the IGN 9/10 Big Walk review . “Falling down a mountain at night and scrambling to find your dropped gear, finding your friends from a flare in the distance, or developing the language to both name things in its world and build a process to figure out its most complex puzzles is all part of the magic that makes Big Walk unlike any other co-op game.”

Other hugely popular 'friendslop' games include Peak, Gamble With Your Friends, Lethal Company, and R.E.P.O., which have enjoyed millions of sales on Steam... and countless clones on the likes of Roblox.

articles.title: Mike Flanagan Teases 'Very Cool and Unexpected On-Ramp' Into the World of Warhammer 40,000 for Henry Cavill's Amazon TV Show
articles.summary: Horror specialist Mike Flanagan has issued an update on his hotly anticipated live-action Warhammer 40,000 TV series starring Henry Cavill, teasing something “unexpected” for fans.
articles.body:
Horror specialist Mike Flanagan has issued an update on his hotly anticipated live-action Warhammer 40,000 TV series, teasing something “unexpected” for fans.

Flanagan has only ever spoken in vague terms about the Warhammer project, dancing around the details while out and about promoting his Prime Video series, Carrie. Last month, he discussed the challenges of adapting Games Workshop’s long-running and complex Warhammer 40,000 universe into a TV show , calling it “brutally difficult.” And in a new interview with Deadline , he said much the same, although did give fans something new to chew on.

Flanagan, writer, director, and showrunner of a number of much-loved Netflix horror TV shows including The Haunting of Hill House, The Haunting of Bly Manor, and The Fall of the House of Usher, said: “Henry Cavill would be furious if I divulged anything about what we’re working on. All I can say is that Warhammer is a fascinating world. The challenge, as anyone familiar with it knows, is finding a way in — it’s so big. There are 700 novels, discounting the [table top] game, the interactive elements and so much of the rest of the lore.”

Warhammer 40,000 11th Edition Cinematic Trailer: All Shots of the Emperor

Despite this challenge, Flanagan insisted he had found “a very cool and unexpected on-ramp into it, which I think is very exciting. I’m sworn to secrecy on all of it, but I’m having the time of my life working on it.”

I’ll get into what this “very cool and unexpected on-ramp” might be below, but for now, some background: Flanagan has signed a multi-year deal with Amazon to develop and produce original series for the studio, the first of which was his adaptation of Stephen King’s horror classic, Carrie. While Carrie Season 2 is confirmed, Flanagan is also working on Warhammer 40,000, which will be part of Henry Cavill’s Warhammer 40,000 Cinematic Universe. The former Superman actor is set to star in the show, although we don’t know which character he will play.

So, what could Flanagan be talking about here? Well, I doubt he’s making a Trazyn the Infinite and Orikan the Diviner sitcom, let’s put it that way. I’ve said before that I think Flanagan will adapt Dan Abnett’s wonderful Eisenhorn series and that Cavill will play Eisenhorn himself , and I'm sticking to my guns.

An Eisenhorn adaptation would, theoretically at least, be tighter in scope than some of the grander Warhammer 40,000 stories, and help keep production manageable. The Eisenhorn Omnibus series does feature Space Marines, but they only make brief and rare appearances. The story focuses heavily on Gregor Eisenhorn and regular humans rather than the giant genetically enhanced warriors.

And I think Eisenhorn would probably fit the bill as something “very cool and unexpected” in terms of an “on-ramp” into the Warhammer 40,000 universe. Because while hardcore fans like me wouldn’t be surprised to see Eisenhorn on Prime Video, your average Warhammer 40,000 fan — or, perhaps put more accurately, your average Space Marine fan — would expect to see Space Marines knocking lumps out of each other. For casual fans who have perhaps played Space Marine 2 or watched the superb Warhammer 40,000 Secret Level animated episode and not delved deeper into the lore, a show about an Inquisitor would be quite “unexpected.”

All the way back in December 2022 (yes, it’s been nearly four years since Games Workshop and Amazon announced their intention to work together), Cavill was said to be “bringing his lore expertise to the mantle of Executive Producer, and his sword arm to the starring role.”

“I have loved Warhammer since I was a boy, making this moment truly special for me. The opportunity to shepherd this cinematic universe from its inception is quite the honour and the responsibility,” Cavill said at the time. “I couldn't be more grateful for all the hard work put in by Vertigo, Amazon and Games Workshop to make this happen. One step closer to making a nigh-on lifelong dream come true.”

articles.title: 'Go Play GTA 6, We Need to Detox,' Wardogs Developer Tells Fans as It Prepares to Take December Off
articles.summary: After the runaway success of Wardogs, a new sandbox multiplayer shooter in Early Access on PC, the team at Bulkhead is taking a well-deserved break. They want you to know you can take a break, too.
articles.body:
After the runaway success of Wardogs , a new sandbox multiplayer shooter in Early Access on PC, the team at Bulkhead is taking a well-deserved break — and they want you to know you can take a break, too.

It’s a break the team likely needs. Since launch, there’s been balance patch after balance patch, hotfixes, major updates, and small updates. Wardogs even saw some controversy when it attempted to region lock players to prevent cheating.

Speaking to Edge Magazine, via GamesRadar , Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer explained the pressure the team had been dealing with. "Everyone has done something that's not in their job description,” Brammer said. “Everyone wears multiple hats, because they can see the path to success with the product."

Following a flurry of updates and a disappointing Wardogs Season 2 launch , Bulkhead is taking the whole month of December off to rest and refresh for the new year and the road to the game’s 1.0 launch.

"We're going to make sure players know they can f**k off in December," he said. "Go play GTA 6 , we need to detox.”

It’s a refreshing approach to hear a developer acknowledge the incoming leviathan that is Rockstar’s open-world crime sequel. Most publishers are just quietly changing their plans with no outward communication, but Bulkhead addressed the massive, massive elephant filling the room.

GTA 6 is out on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox, and it is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time. A number of publishers and developers either worked to release their games beforehand, leading to the September crunch, or push them back into early 2027. Star Citizen chief Chris Roberts claimed he delayed spinoff Squadron 42 into next year because he didn't want it going up against the "attention buzz saw of GTA 6."

"While GTA 6 isn’t launching on PC this November, pretty much all outlets and most content creators will be all over it, not leaving a lot of room for other coverage," Roberts continued.

Analysts expect GTA 6 will make over $5 billion in launch week alone , so expect it to fill your feeds for a few weeks.

articles.title: Wild Horse Nine Is a Great Hang, With Beautifully Nuanced Performances From Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich
articles.summary: Review: Wild Horse Nine is a great hang. The script is one of Martin McDonagh's best, complemented by Rockwell's and Malkovich's beautifully nuanced performances.
articles.body:
Wild Horse Nine is in theaters on Nov. 6.

Two killers head out on a not quite break-from-work trip to a picturesque location, where shenanigans ensue. I've seen that movie and it's called In Bruges, you might be saying. But In Bruges writer-director Martin McDonagh is far from playing the same Funny Games as Michael Haneke by making the same film twice, so while his new film Wild Horse Nine might put him in familiar territory, this is not just another In Bruges -- and we are all the better for it.

The Catholic guilt remains, but McDonagh trades the tortured hitmen of In Bruges for two CIA spooks who need a reprieve from setting up Augusto Pinochet's coup in early '70s Chile. So off they go for a quick breather from working to overthrow a democratically elected Marxist (the CIA can't have that, no. Definitely not in their own hemisphere!) to see the big heads on Easter Island.

What makes this film great is its ability to tackle heady subjects like political violence and CIA-backed regime change and yet still be funny as hell and a great hangout movie. It's a tough needle to thread, but Martin McDonagh does it without being insensitive to the real-world changes that are happening around his characters.

McDonagh is an excellent filmmaker, but he’s undoubtedly best at screenwriting. His dialogue is incredible. It can be absurd, funny, charming, mean, and insightful; most of the time, it can be all of those at once. I've been using some form of "You're a nice guy, Pádraic" as my preferred euphemism for calling people an idiot ever since I saw The Banshees of Inisherin . It's such a nice, pleasant veneer, but it's so cutting. And when I use it, most people don't realize I'm insulting them, just like Pádraic.

Wild Horse Nine is also chock-full of great zingers. Take the scene in the trailer, where Lee (Sam Rockwell) is trying to shush Chris (John Malkovich), who won't stop talking about all his political assassinations.

Chris snaps back, "I've killed people in countries you can't even spell," and then mentions that he killed a guy in Czechoslovakia.

"You never killed anyone in Czechosl-fucking-vakia. You just know I can't spell it," responds Lee.

Those micro-tugs-of-war for power, jockeying for a kind of dominance that's ultimately inconsequential, are a hallmark of McDonagh's writing and what make his dialogue so memorable. It's part lyrical, part petty, and even takes on elements of stand-up comedy like the callback.

For example, some of the film's best jokes are set up early with pithy lines, only to be paid off later. And in a true test of a film's quality, McDonagh didn't burn off the best moments of dialogue in the trailer.

Of course, McDonagh's dialogue is only half the equation. A script is only as good as the hands of the performers it's in, and McDonagh has assembled a great cast.

Sam Rockwell is back, collaborating with the director who helped him win his Oscar for 2018's Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri . This time he's playing Lee, a spy whose loyalty is torn between his partner and his agency.

John Malkovich co-stars as Lee's partner and the more seasoned spy, Chris. The CIA was doing tons of meddling in the '60s and '70s, and Chris was boots on the ground for a lot of it. All that experience combined with his wildcard nature is what's pushing Steve Buscemi's MJ (the head of the CIA's South American operations) to believe he's a real liability and insist, "He ain't leaving the fuckin' island." (Can you blame the guy? He's talking about killing people... on an airplane.)

Lee and Chris's relationship is a cockeyed mix of Obi-Wan and Anakin and part Riggs and Murtaugh. Malkovich's Chris is both the old, grizzled Murtaugh and the maverick Riggs combined into one CIA spy. Meanwhile, Lee is the well-meaning Padawan who is on the verge of having to make some hard decisions.

Whether Chris is pontificating on why "gay countries make the best cheese" or clowning on Lee for all his wife's infidelities, Malkovich has most of the film's best lines. (Speaking of which, Parker Posey is absolutely hilarious as Lee's wife Margie.) Listening to these two bicker is the absolute best part of the film. That's all thanks to Malkovich and Rockwell's chemistry, which makes these scenes feel like the effortless banter of old colleagues.

Quips aside, Malkovich deftly handles a complex, multifaceted character with empathy and charm. Without getting into too much detail, Chris knows he isn't long for this world, and, like the flawed Catholic he is, he's seeking a bit of redemption on his way out. He's said some bad things, done some worse things; his ability to piss off literally every character in the film is unrivaled. But Malkovich's charisma keeps us invested in him, and by the end, we're rooting for him.

The film's redemptive tension is best exemplified by Chris's relationship with Monica, one of the young progressive women he insults at the airport. Played by Chilean actress Mariana di Girolamo, Monica is essentially the heart of the film. Despite being completely repulsed by Chris's antics, they keep running into each other on the island, and eventually it's Monica who really forces Chris to confront his past and draw out what's left of his humanity.

I can't help but compare this film to In Bruges. In many superficial ways, they're extremely similar, but the comparison also helps emphasize how much Martin McDonagh has improved as a storyteller. It's not like he was bad before; In Bruges, with its funny but generic hitmen on the lam, was one of the better aughts crime flicks that were trying to duplicate Pulp Fiction's success over a decade later.

Wild Horse Nine and In Bruges share themes of guilt, redemption, moral codes, and loyalty. But where In Bruges confines its moral reckoning to the personal, grounding Wild Horse Nine in historical events adds an extra layer of thematic depth. Using the lead-up to Pinochet's coup as the backdrop for Lee and Chris's misadventures on Easter Island forces the characters to confront the moral culpability of their actions, while also challenging American audiences to reckon with the enduring consequences of their country's political meddling.

To put a finer point on it, it's extremely tough for a film to have me laughing at two CIA agents debate who would be a bigger security risk to the agency, a boozer wife or a heroin wife, and also get me to wiki Patrice Lumumba immediately after walking out of the theater. But that's what makes Wild Horse Nine stand out: it makes the absurdity of these men entertaining without letting you forget the very real consequences of their work.

Cinematography That Evokes a '70s Aesthetic

If you're like me, you go see a Martin McDonagh film for the script and the performances. But make no mistake, Wild Horse Nine is a beautifully photographed film, even if there’s nothing outstanding about its cinematography. McDonagh and cinematographer Ben Davis really lean into the time period's '70s aesthetic. Some of the film's shots were made to look like they were came from Lee's Super 8 camera, and even have the edges of the stock in frame. The film's establishing shots, especially those featuring the island's iconic moai (the big heads), are rendered beautifully in a grainy, hypersaturated film stock.

Visually, the film makes the most out of its locations in the same way an Italian chef makes the most out of their ingredients. Bear with me here a second. Originally, I wanted to say the film's cinematography was too workmanlike, but that's too harsh. To better understand the film's photographic choices, we need to examine the differences between the philosophies of French and Italian cooking.

For those unaware, French cooking takes a more maximalist approach, emphasizing the chef's skill and the complex methods they use to prepare an ingredient, while Italian cooking emphasizes minimalism, drawing focus to the quality of an ingredient by preparing it using the simplest methods.

While McDonagh and Davis take the Italian chef approach to their framing, getting out of the way of some truly magnificent vistas, they still have some tricks up their sleeves, progressively increasing their use of close-ups as the film gets more and more intimate with the characters. Despite these almost subliminal techniques, the camerawork never really adds a level of flair that would make it stand out.

articles.title: 'Horror Is Always at Its Strongest When Something Bad Is Happening to the World' – Boss of Silent Hill Remake Dev Bloober Reveals the Secret to His Studio's Success
articles.summary: Bloober Team certainly appears to be the busiest horror studio in the business right now. Off the back of its 2024 Silent Hill 2 remake selling over 5 million copies, the Polish developer currently has a staggering seven horror games in various stages of production. During Gamescom Asia x Thailand Game Show in Bangkok last week, IGN sat down with Bloober Team CEO Piotr Babieno to get an insight into the secrets to his studio’s success, its ambitious plans for the future, and why horror has become such a bankable genre in recent years.
articles.body:
Bloober Team certainly appears to be the busiest horror studio in the business right now. Off the back of its 2024 Silent Hill 2 remake selling over 5 million copies, the Polish developer currently has a staggering seven horror games in various stages of production. During Gamescom Asia x Thailand Game Show in Bangkok last week, IGN sat down with Bloober Team CEO Piotr Babieno to get an insight into the secrets to his studio’s success, its ambitious plans for the future, and why horror has become such a bankable genre in recent years.

“I would say that horror is always at its strongest when something bad is happening to the world,” said Babieno. “When we have climate changes, when we have wars, [or] when we have some economical issues in the world. This is the moment when society [has] some kind of fear inside.”

“That’s why horror movies, horror novels, and horror games are working so well," he continued. "It’s working for horror, but I’m not happy about it because it always means that the world is not in good shape.”

Babieno is obviously not wrong. Humanity is currently faced with a global cost of living crisis, increasingly volatile weather events, ongoing wars between Russia and Ukraine and the U.S. and Iran, and the existential threat posed by the rapidly accelerating adoption of AI across virtually every major industry.

At the same time, the horror genre has rarely been hotter across most entertainment mediums. Indie horror films Backrooms and Obsession became major success stories at the box office earlier this year, with the latter going on to make over half a billion dollars. The Resident Evil series continues to be one of the most dominant brands in the genre, with its latest video game instalment Resident Evil Requiem selling 8.5 million copies since its launch in February, and its latest big screen adaptation from Weapons director Zach Cregger quickly becoming the highest-grossing Resident Evil movie ever .

The surging popularity of spooks and scares has also spread to many popular streaming services. Mike Flanagan’s adaptation of Stephen King’s Carrie performing strong enough on Prime Video in order to be renewed for a second season . Friday the 13th prequel series Crystal Lake has apparently become one of Peacock’s biggest scripted original series. Meanwhile Apple’s Widows Bay is one of the most celebrated TV shows of the year – horror or otherwise – snaring a whopping 14 Emmy Awards in September.

Even comic book movies are turning to the genre, with the DCU’s thoroughly disturbing Clayface enjoying a strong opening weekend in October . Public domain characters have also proved to be ripe for the picking, with two Winnie the Pooh slasher movies already released and a third one on the way in January .

However, Bloober Team is no bandwagon-jumper. Although the foundational years of the studio were spent producing a mix of casual games and contract work, the developer has been singularly focussed on becoming a specialist house of horror since it launched Layers of Fear in 2016. In the decade since, Bloober has steadily risen to become one of the most trusted conjurers of fear and dread in videogames, proving to be equally adept at reimagining licensed properties as it is at establishing new IPs of its own.

“There are a lot of great horror game developers in the world; we are one of them,” said Babieno. “We’re trying to focus [purely] on creating horror so that’s why the iteration process allows us to work not just on the formula [for creating fear], but on the technological aspect of creating games.”

“Also understanding our fans. Understanding what we did wrong and how we could improve. Project by project we are always thinking, ‘is this the next step for the studio? Is this the next step for our fans?’ Because if it’s not, you don’t want to waste four years of your life creating a new title.”

While Babieno’s team has become attuned to listening to its dedicated fanbase, it’s also learned to ignore its detractors online. Not unlike the undeserved backlash that Zach Cregger was forced to endure prior to the release of his Resident Evil movie , Bloober Team faced plenty of scrutiny from Silent Hill diehards when it was hard at work remaking Silent Hill 2. However, Babieno makes it clear that his team had complete confidence in their ability to reimagine the Konami classic to a standard that would be embraced by even its harshest of critics.

“At the beginning we suffered a lot of hate from fans,” said Babieno. “But we did the one thing which any studio who is trying to create something great is able to do: focus on the project, focus on delivering the best quality game, and put the noise around it out of our head.”

“So this is what we tried to do; we believed from the very beginning that we’d be able to achieve this and it happened. Silent Hill 2 was a pivot point for Bloober Team.”

Silent Hill 2’s subsequent critical and commercial success is likely a big part of the reason that Bloober Team now finds itself in such hot demand and experiencing a period of expansion at a time when so many other studios in the industry are suffering cuts and closures. Bloober Team is currently composed of two first-party studios, and has recently added the second-party Broken Mirror Games, a label that it uses to co-develop games with five other Polish development teams. A remake of the original Silent Hill, Layers of Fear 3, Nintendo Switch 2-exclusive Onyx: The Dark Grip, and Star Trek: Shadow Frontier, a psychological horror game set in Gene Roddenberry’s beloved sci-fi universe, are four of the seven games currently in development that have been confirmed so far.

Babieno was unable to comment on the recent Silent Hill leak that suggested it would be released in 2027 and star Gabrielle Fritz and Jade Matthew – when prompted, he dismissed the details as "rumors." He also couldn’t reveal much about Star Trek: Shadow Frontier, other than agreeing with publishing partner Paramount Games Studio’s goals for it to be “the best Star Trek game of all time,” by stating simply that he wouldn’t be working on it if he “didn’t have such a fight.”

However, Babieno was keen to share his enthusiasm for Project H, the working title for the next game from the team behind 2025’s Cronos: The New Dawn. Although according to Babieno the project is only in the late stages of pre-production, he seems confident that it will represent yet another stride forward for the studio.

“This project is like a huge step from Cronos and from our previous titles so it will deliver a new kind of experience,” said Babieno. “But at the same time it will be very familiar to everyone who [has] already played Bloober Team games. So we will still keep our DNA in it, but we will show this in a completely fresh new way.”

Ultimately for Babieno, the ambition for Bloober Team and where it sits in the booming horror genre seems clear.

“I love Silent Hill and Resident Evil, and I feel that there is a place for a third huge horror IP as well,” said Babieno. “I think we’re on the right track with everything we’re creating. You can feel that Bloober Team’s games are a little bit different [to] those that are already available on the market.”

“The most important [goal] for me is to set new milestones in the game industry.”

Bloober Team’s next release is DLC for Cronos: The New Dawn. Dubbed Cronos: Lazarus, this story expansion serves as a prequel to the events of the main game and will apparently present players with a “faster, more aggressive style of combat.” Cronos: Lazarus is set to release on December 3 for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC, with the Nintendo Switch 2 version launching sometime in early 2027.

Tristan Ogilvie is a senior video editor at IGN based in Sydney, Australia. He has 25 years of experience covering video games, having served as Deputy Editor on Official PlayStation 2 Magazine Australia and as Editor of Official Xbox 360 Magazine Australia, before joining IGN in 2009. articles.title: Indie Game Storefront Itch Deletes a 'Couple of Terabytes of AI Slop,' Adds 'No AI' Filter to Search Results
articles.summary: Itch has clamped down on the deluge of low effort generative AI games flooding its store, confirming the removal of a couple of terabytes of "AI slop."
articles.body:
Itch has clamped down on the deluge of low effort generative AI games flooding its store, confirming the removal of a couple of terabytes of "AI slop."

In a statement on social media , the indie game storefront said it had begun the process of removing thousands of AI games and other marketplace items, including asset packs for game developers, due to spam. “Just deleted a couple terabytes of AI slop,” Itch said.

"Just because you can upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models doesn't mean you should upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models," Itch continued .

Itch has also added generative AI disclosure filtering to its website, including on its search results page "in order to better control what you see." Via the 'No AI' filter, users can strip out games with AI disclosures.

When asked if this was a blanket ban on generative AI, Itch said it’s only against the site’s terms and conditions when it comes to spam. “Avoid uploading excessive amounts of automatically generated or AI-generated content,” the site’s official terms and conditions states. AI generated content is fine if it’s “clearly stated in your project description and that it adds substantial value to the user experience.” Multiple iterations of the same thing spat out with slight variations are against the rules, and AI content has to have some sense of curation to pass the store’s guidelines.

Itch has taken a stronger stance on AI than, for example, Valve. While Steam has an AI discosure policy for store pages, Valve does not limit AI-focused developer access to its platform, nor block "AI slop" from from it despite complaints from fans and developers about the deluge of low effort games that flooded the recent Steam Next Fest . Valve also put the onus on developers to ensure their game stands out amid the detritus. In particular, there’s been a big issue on Steam of developers having their games instantly cloned with AI as soon as they share any development progress.

"Rather than relying on a single mechanic that someone can easily copy, you need to keep growing your game by adding features, personality, and creativity that stem from your own perspective," Valve’s Tom Giardino said.

Epic Games, on the other hand, is all-in on AI. Its boss, Tim Sweeney, has heavily criticized Valve for its AI disclosure policy , calling it a "political act."
